analysis.one_liner: Adds a new 5-20% surtax on individual income above $350,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in the Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a new surtax on top of existing income taxes for individuals with very high incomes: 5% on income over $350,000, 10% over $500,000, 15% over $1 million, and 20% over $10 million, with the thresholds adjusted for inflation each year [S2][S3]. It was introduced in October 2011, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and received no further action of any kind [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the direct beneficiaries would have been the federal treasury and, indirectly, anyone who benefits from reduced deficits or from whatever the revenue was later spent on — the bill itself raised revenue without designating a use. More precisely, the bill shifted a portion of the tax burden onto the roughly 1% of taxpayers with incomes above $350,000. Households below that threshold would have paid nothing under the surtax [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a progressive surtax on top of existing income tax, starting at 5% on modified adjusted gross income above $350,000 and rising to 20% above $10 million, so only high-income households pay it [S2][S3].
Adjusts the income thresholds for inflation after 2011, preventing the tax from gradually reaching middle-income households over time [S2][S3].
Applies to individuals, estates, and trusts but not corporations, targeting personal income rather than business income [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, individual taxpayers with modified adjusted gross income above $350,000 — roughly the top 1-2% of earners — would have paid the new surtax, with the largest bills falling on households above $1 million and especially above $10 million. Notably, the bill defines income as adjusted gross income minus the deduction for investment interest, meaning investors who borrow to invest would shield some income from the surtax [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill raises revenue but designates no use for it — no spending program, no deficit-reduction mechanism, and no offset elsewhere in the tax code — so its practical benefit to ordinary people is indirect and unspecified [S3].

The carve-out for the investment interest deduction means leveraged investors — those who borrow against assets to generate income — would pay the surtax on a reduced base, sparing some of the very highest-income households the bill is nominally aimed at [S2][S3].

A good-faith objection: stacking a surtax on top of regular rates raises the top marginal tax burden substantially, which critics argue could discourage investment and entrepreneurship among the affected group; the bill text itself avoids treating the surtax as a rate change for certain credit and minimum-tax purposes, a sign of drafting complexity [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted real tax burden onto high-income households, with thresholds indexed to inflation so it would not creep down into the middle class. Its main weaknesses are that it channels revenue to no specific purpose, and that the investment-interest deduction lets leveraged investors shield part of their income. As drafted, it is a straightforwardly progressive revenue measure with modest design flaws, not a comprehensive tax reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alcee Hastings introduced the bill on October 5, 2011, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
No cosponsor signed on at any point [S4].
The committee took no further action; the bill's only recorded steps after referral were the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record [S5].
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without ever reaching the House floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households were better off because the bill died: no new surtax was ever imposed, and the top rates in effect at the time remained unchanged. The Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, faced no political cost for the inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households, whose taxes stayed unchanged

for.name: Rep. Alcee L. Hastings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, but recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no markup, no hearing, no vote — letting the bill expire at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Democrats
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill with no visible support even within the sponsor's own party.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to reveal a partisan split, and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so it never assembled enough support to register as a partisan fight.

industries.note: The bill's entire cost falls on this group through a new 5-20% surtax. Its interest in the bill failing ran against any use of the revenue for the public.

The bill excludes the investment interest deduction from the tax base, so investors who borrow to invest would pay less than other high earners. This carve-out shrinks the burden on some of the wealthiest filers while leaving it on salaried high earners.
